scenes.name: One — The Ruts

images.name: the ruts
images.file: Misty Mountain Outpost Gate at Dawn.png

scenes.body:
Indented notes are the DM's alone, and each one is a place to stop reading.
**A ↳ heading is a condition — read what follows it only if that happens, and where two sit together read one side, not both. Everything else is read aloud.**

---

Elmar Barthen catches you on the way past his door and does not waste any of it on pleasantries.

**BARTHEN:** "Eleven days ago I sent a cart east to the dwarves at the excavation. Standing order — flour, nails, lamp oil, salt pork, same as every month. Tam Hollis was driving it. Nineteen, thin, talks a great deal, works for me.

Four days out and four days back is the run. He has had eleven. I have asked every single person who has come in off that road since and not one of them has passed a cart going either way.

I cannot pay you in coin. There is not much coin in this town before spring and what there is I need. What I can do is open my account to you — anything off these shelves, no bill, for as long as you are working out of Phandalin. In a winter where nobody can get rope, that is worth more than money and we both know it.

Bring my cart back. Bring the lad back first."


> - [ ] The shape of the night: a spear puts Amryn down, Serrin heals her and travels with them, the ruin opens under the shaft, the basilisk and the arch arrive together, the disguise comes off halfway through the fight, Caelus goes through, and the whole place comes down behind him. Nobody in the party dies.

---

You find the tracks before you are out of sight of the palisade, and they are easy to hold. Barthen's cart runs an iron-shod wheel with a chip out of the rim, and every third turn of it presses a small clean comma into the frozen mud, and once you have seen that comma once you will not lose it again all day.

For an hour the road behaves. It climbs out of the valley in long patient switchbacks through black pine, and as it climbs the air thins and sharpens and begins to taste of nothing at all, and the smell of the town — woodsmoke, wet wool, the tannery behind Barthen's — falls away below you until there is only cold stone and the working of four horses and the small sounds of your own gear.

Then the pines thin out, and stop, and the country opens in front of you like a held breath.

It is enormous and it is white and it is utterly still. The snowfields roll away north and east in long slow swells, broken here and there by the black stitching of a hedge or the grey knuckle of a boulder standing out of the drift, and above all of it the sky is the flat pale colour of skimmed milk. There is no wind — not a breath, not a stir in the snow-crust, nothing moving anywhere in the whole visible world — and because nothing is moving, the sound of your horses goes out across all that open ground and does not come back.

The ruts run out ahead into the white, eleven days old and crisp as the day they were cut, and nothing has come along behind them to break them. No rider. No walker. Not one other cart, in eleven days, on the only road east out of Phandalin.

Far to the north, over the shoulder of everything else on the horizon, Icespire Peak wears weather of its own: a flat grey cloud sitting hard down on the summit like a lid pressed onto a pot. It has not moved or thinned or changed shape in the three days you have been able to see it. Every single person you asked about that in Phandalin gave you the same shrug. It is always like that. It has always been like that. None of them could tell you why it should not be.

> - [ ] Open road, no threat yet. Room here for an order of march and for the party to talk.

The first farm you pass stands back from the road behind a drystone wall with the gate pulled shut and pegged.

The shutters have been closed from inside and the door latched from without. There is no smoke over the chimney and no dog in the yard, and the snow lying between the wall and the step is smooth and blue-shadowed and entirely unbroken. By the well there is a wooden bucket with an inch of grey ice standing in it, and the rope has frozen stiff on the windlass.

A mile further on, where the land falls away west of the road, a charcoal burner has built a stack and banked it and capped it with turf and then walked away from it. The turf is still sitting square on the crown where a careful man put it. The whole thing has gone stone cold.

Seven days and seven nights of work goes into a stack like that, tended in shifts, never once left alone from the lighting to the drawing. And then left alone.

| When | Check | DC | What they get |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anyone goes over the wall and into the yard | Perception | any | Latched from the outside, not barred from within. Whoever did it had a key in their hand and expected to want it again |
| | | 12 | Emptied properly. No food, no tools, no blankets, no coin, no stock, no feed. That is hours of work, not minutes. Nobody fled this house — they packed it |
| | | 16 | Inside the doorpost there is a column of knife-scratches, a child's height marked off year on year. The topmost one is fresh, and somebody has cut it out of the wood and taken the piece with them |

> - [ ] Open floor at the farm. Nothing in the house is worth carrying off and nothing is waiting in it — the paragraph below is for anyone who goes inside, and the ride east resumes when they have had enough of it.

Inside, the place has been stripped to the walls. Two rooms and a loft, a cold hearth swept out properly, pale rectangles on the boards where furniture stood, and four hooks by the door with nothing hanging on them.

Mid-morning, Kaelen puts a hand up and swings down out of the saddle before anybody has asked her why, because the ground has started telling a different story.

Something has crossed the road ahead of you. Not travelled along it — crossed it, at an angle, coming down off the northern slope and carrying on south into open country without once pausing at the verge. Six sets of prints, and every one of them is pressed down on top of Barthen's wheel-ruts.

She crouches over the nearest of them for a while without saying anything, and then she says it.

**KAELEN:** "Orcs. Six."

She does not sound pleased about being right.

| When | Check | DC | What they get |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anyone gets down off a horse and puts a hand in one of the prints | Survival | any | Bare feet, broad across the ball, toes driven in hard at the front of the step. Orcs — six of them, going south with weight on their backs |
| | | 11 | Two days old against eleven for the ruts. Barthen's cart was long gone before any of this came through |
| | | 15 | Far too much baggage for a raiding party, and two of the six are small, short-strided, and being hurried along between the others |
| Somebody turns and looks back up the slope they came down | Perception | any | Open rising ground, bare and blue with shadow, empty to the skyline |
| | | 13 | A thin brown stain low on the sky a long way north. Something up there has been burning for days and not one person has gone to look |

> - [ ] The road is theirs for a few minutes. The ride carries on when somebody decides to stay on the ruts rather than follow the trail south.

There is nothing south of here that an orc could want. Nothing to raid, nothing worth carrying off, nothing to eat that is not easier to find where they came from. They are not travelling toward anything.

Which leaves the direction they came from. Something is up there, somewhere under that brown stain on the sky, and orcs do not walk away from anything they believe they can fight.

> - [ ] The orcs are established. A quiet mile sits between the crossing and the ambush.

You ride on, and you are all watching the slopes now instead of the road.

It is the horses that notice first. A mile past the crossing, all four of them come up at once without being asked, ears forward, breath going up in fast clouds, and they will not settle. Nothing moves on the snowfield to the north. Nothing moves anywhere. But the horses are looking at a fold in the ground about forty yards off the road where the land dips and you cannot see the bottom of it.

And then the ground gives them up all at once.

Five orcs come up out of that dip at a dead run, grey-green and steaming in the cold air, and they do not shout and they do not posture, which is somehow much worse than if they had. They come in a loose spread with their weight well forward, three driving straight at the middle of you and two swinging wide. A sixth stays back in the rocks above the dip with a bow already drawn.

The one coming up on the left has a spear — a long one, iron-headed, carried low and level — and it is not slowing for Levi at all. It comes past his shoulder and inside his reach, and whatever he does about that on the way past, it does not stop, and it keeps going for the one of you who is not wearing any armour.

> - [ ] Three in, two wide, archer at range and moving each round. The spear-carrier ignores everything else to reach Amryn, and it connects. She goes down. Not dead — down.

The spear goes in through Amryn's back and out under her ribs, and the orc puts a boot on her shoulder to drag it free, and the fight goes on over the top of her.

When it ends there is a hard ringing silence across all that white, and your breath going up in clouds, and six bodies steaming in the snow, and Amryn face down and not moving in a spreading red patch that is already freezing at the edges.

And from the road behind you, a voice says, perfectly calmly:

**A VOICE BEHIND YOU:** "Don't move her. Let me."

---

scenes.name: Two — Serrin
scenes.body:
There is a man walking up the road from the west. He is perhaps a hundred yards back and closing at a steady unhurried walk, as though he has been a quarter of a mile behind you since Phandalin and has only now caught up, and none of you saw him on the open road all morning.

He is a high elf, and he is dressed in white — a long travelling robe, heavy, plainly cut, belted with grey cord, and somehow clean in a country where nothing has been clean for a month. He carries no pack worth the name. There is no weapon anywhere on him that you can see. His face is pleasant, and unremarkable, and of the kind you will find you cannot describe an hour from now even though you are looking directly at it.

He walks past all of you without hurrying, kneels down in the red snow beside Amryn, and lays two fingers against the side of her throat.

**THE STRANGER:** "Spear. In through the back, out under the ribs. It has missed the lung, which is the only reason we are having this conversation. She is extremely lucky and she is not going to feel lucky for about a week."

He puts one hand flat between her shoulder blades and says three words that none of you catch, and the bleeding does not slow down. It stops. Amryn's breath comes back into her with the sound of somebody surfacing out of deep water.

He sits back on his heels and looks up at the rest of you.

**THE STRANGER:** "Serrin. I am going east and so are you, and the road has orcs on it, so I would rather we went together than separately. Is that acceptable to you, or would you like to discuss it while she is lying in the snow?"

> - [ ] Open floor the moment he says his name — this is where they interrogate him, and the conditions below answer whatever they put to him. He is not asking to come. He is being reasonable loudly enough that refusing him is the unreasonable act.

> - [ ] Refused outright, he shrugs, wishes them well and walks east at his own pace — and he is sitting at the dwarves' fire when they arrive, with nobody there finding it strange. Everything below happens either way.

#### ↳ If they ask who he is

**SERRIN:** "A healer, out of the west. Three months on this coast and none of them warm."

#### ↳ If they ask where he is going

**SERRIN:** "The same place you are, as it happens. I was in Barthen's two days ago and I heard a man complaining about dwarves who had broken into something old and stopped answering their post. Old things are the only subject I was ever any use at. So — east."

#### ↳ If they ask about payment

**SERRIN:** "No."

#### ↳ And when they push

**SERRIN:** "No, and I would rather you did not keep offering. It makes the next few days awkward and we have a long way to walk."

#### ↳ If they ask whether he is afraid of the orcs

He looks at the six bodies in the snow for a moment, and then at whoever asked, and smiles very slightly, and does not answer the question at all.

| When | Check | DC | What they get |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anyone takes a proper look at him while he talks | Insight | any | Composed, courteous, and not remotely surprised by a road with six dead orcs on it |
| | | 13 | Every word out of him is true. He is simply saying very little of it |
| | | 17 | The gaps are deliberate and well worn. He has given this account before, more than once, and it has been trimmed |
| | | 20 | He has been watching one of you since before the fighting started, and it is not the wizard bleeding in the snow. It is Levi |
| Anyone with the training watches him close the wound | Arcana | any | Three words and a flat hand. No components, no holy symbol, no gesture worth the name |
| | | 12 | Not a prayer and not any spell on any list you were taught to recite |
| | | 16 | It cost him nothing. Not a slot, not a breath — he spent no more doing that than you spend closing a door |
| Levi looks at the man's face at any point | — | free | Nothing at all. No pull of recognition, no itch, no half-memory. And out of everything about him, that is the only part that is strange |

> - [ ] Open floor. Serrin answers anything put to him, and the journey resumes once the party settle whether he walks with them or behind them.

Once there is time to go through what is lying in the snow, there is not much, and what there is does not sit right.

Eleven gold and some silver between the six of them, and one serviceable hatchet worth keeping. Four days of hard bread and nothing else to eat at all. Two cook pots, both mended. Six bedrolls, for six orcs, which is six more than any raiding party on this coast has ever carried. And in the pack belonging to the one with the bow, wrapped in cloth and carried rather than worn, a child's carved horse with the paint worn off the nose.

Strung on a plaited cord around that same one's neck, tucked down inside the furs where it would sit against the skin, there is a scale the length of your hand. Frost-blue, going almost white along the thin edge, drilled neatly through near the base. One face of it has been rubbed smooth and slightly cloudy, the way a thing goes when a thumb has been over it and over it, in the dark, for luck.

Nobody takes a trophy off a dragon. You take a charm off a dragon — and you wear a charm like that against your skin because you have seen the thing close enough to count its teeth and you would very much like it not to see you again.

> - [ ] On the orcs: 11 gp, a little silver, a serviceable hatchet, and the scale. The scale is worth nothing to a merchant and a great deal to anybody in Phandalin who has been saying there is no dragon.

#### ↳ If they let him travel with them

He is good company on a road, which nobody expects.

He asks Kaelen how she read the crossing, and when she tells him he asks a second question that proves he was listening to the first answer. He asks Emeric what he plays, and listens to the whole of it without once looking at anything else. He carries his share of the watch that night without being asked, and wakes whoever is next exactly when he said he would.

He does not ask Levi one single question the entire way.

#### ↳ If they send him on his way

He takes it without any argument at all. He gets up, brushes the snow off the white robe, tells you he hopes the wizard mends clean, and walks east past you at the same unhurried pace he came up the road at.

By the time you have the horses sorted he is a white mark a long way ahead of you on the road, and then he is over the rise, and then he is not there at all.

> - [ ] Either way, he is at the dig before them and the rest of the session runs the same.


---

scenes.name: Three — The Dig
scenes.body:
The ruts leave the road late the following morning at a cairn with a claim marker nailed to a post, and run down a rough cut track into a shallow bowl lying between two hills.

The dig is visible from the ridge above and it looks like a wound that somebody has been keeping open on purpose.

A long trench has been driven into the hillside and widened as it went, the walls stepped back in benches so the whole thing descends in rough steps, and at the deep end of it there is a timbered shaft going straight down into the dark. The spoil has been thrown up along both lips of the trench in sorted runs — broken stone in one heap, soil in another, gravel in a third — and every one of those heaps has been squared at the ends and dressed flat along the top. Somebody has been keeping this place tidy for two seasons the way a soldier keeps a kit tidy, which is to say without expecting anyone to notice.

Drawn up beside a lean-to at the trench mouth, with its shafts down and its tarp lashed tight against the weather, there is a cart. The wheels are iron-shod. There is a chip out of one rim.

It is empty, and it has been empty a while. Under the lean-to beside it a brown horse stands up to its hocks in clean straw, blanketed and groomed and recently shod, and somebody has been looking after it properly for a good while.

There are three dwarves in the bowl.

Two of them are working the rock face at the near end of the trench, well apart from one another, each with their own pick and their own patch of stone. Neither is talking. One is a broad dwarf woman with her sleeves cut off at the shoulder in weather that does not warrant it, swinging hard and badly, the way people swing when the work is pointless and they know it. The only sound in the entire hollow of the hill is a pick, and a pause, and a pick, and a pause, and the double knock of it coming back off the far slope a moment afterward.

The third is not working. He is sitting on an upturned crate at the lip of the shaft with his back to the track, facing down into the hole. He is older than the other two by a long way, grey through the beard and heavy in the shoulders, wearing a coat that was good ten years ago, and he has a pipe in one hand that he has not lit and from the look of it has not lit for some time.

Not one of the three stops as you come down the slope. Not one of them calls out.

All three of them have seen you.

#### ↳ If they sent him on ahead

There is a fourth figure in the bowl, and he is the only one who is not working.

Serrin is sitting at the fire outside the lean-to with his boots off and his hands around a cup, in no apparent hurry about anything, and when he sees you come over the lip he raises the cup an inch in greeting and does not get up. Nobody at this camp appears to find it strange that he is here, or to have asked him how he got here first on foot, and the older dwarf does not so much as glance at him.

**SERRIN:** "They have a stew on. It is mostly turnip, and it is hot, and there is enough."

> - [ ] Nobody at the dig can account for him arriving ahead of mounted riders, and nobody has thought to try.

> - [ ] Open floor as they come down into the bowl — the cart is the first thing anybody goes to. It and the well-kept horse close off the obvious dark reading before anyone can raise it. In the cart bed: a folded blanket and a waterskin, and nothing else.

The old one speaks without turning round.

**DON-JON:** "You'll be Barthen's."

He does not turn round. The woman at the face does, and stops swinging, and leans on the pick to watch.

**DON-JON:** "Gerda. Keep at it."

**GERDA:** "There's nothing to keep at."

**DON-JON:** "Keep at it anyway.""

And before anyone can answer:

**DON-JON:** "Took him long enough. I have had a horse of his eating my oats for eleven days and no way of sending word that wasn't the lad himself."

Then he does turn round, and looks at the lot of you, taking his time about it, one face at a time.

**DON-JON:** "Don-Jon Raskin. I run this claim, for as long as anybody lets me. There's stew on the fire and you're welcome to it, and the answer to the question you came to ask is yes, he's here.

Sort of."

#### ↳ When they ask what that means

**DON-JON:** "Went down the shaft yesterday morning with Dazlyn. Her idea and his enthusiasm — she wanted a second pair of hands and a second lamp and he had been pestering her about it for a week.

They have not come back up."

He says that flatly and then stops talking, because that is the whole of the answer to the question he was asked.

> - [ ] Don-Jon does not lie and does not volunteer. He answers the question in front of him completely, then stops. Everything else has to be asked for.

#### ↳ If they ask what is down there

**DON-JON:** "Dwarf-work. Old dwarf-work — older than anything standing between here and the mountains, and better built than any of it. We came down through the roof of it in the autumn and we did not mean to. Put a pick through a ceiling and fell four feet into a room that nobody had stood in since before there was a Phandalin.

There's rooms down there. A lot of them. We have been three months opening them one at a time and Dazlyn has been down every day of it, and she comes up at night talking about things I cannot follow."

#### ↳ If they ask why the other two are up here and not down there

**DON-JON:** "Because I told them to be."

#### ↳ And if they press him on it

**DON-JON:** "There is something living in the lower rooms. We have never seen it. We have seen what it leaves behind."

#### ↳ When they ask what it leaves

**DON-JON:** "Dust. Grit, like somebody's been at the floor with a broom. And there's a boot standing in the third room down that nobody has ever come back for. Upright. Laces still tied."

| When | Check | DC | What they get |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anyone watches the old dwarf rather than listening to him | Insight | any | He is frightened, and not one part of it is for himself |
| | | 12 | He has been counting the hours since yesterday morning, out loud, to nobody, and he is still doing it under the conversation |
| | | 16 | He has already decided he goes down there himself tonight if you will not. He is sixty-one years old and he knows exactly what that means |
| Anyone gives Gerda two minutes and the smallest amount of sympathy | Persuasion | any | She is sick to the back teeth of this claim and glad of somebody new to say it to |
| | | 11 | Two of the crew walked off in the autumn without stopping to collect their pay, and she has never once blamed them for it |
| | | 15 | She has not been past the third room since. Neither has Don-Jon. Only Dazlyn goes deep, and she goes alone, and nobody stops her |
| Anyone asks what Dazlyn is actually doing down there | — | free | Three months, every single day, and she comes up at night talking about dwarvish grammar to people who want their supper |

> - [ ] Open floor at the trench mouth — stew, questions, and the two dwarves at the face. It closes when somebody says out loud that they are going down. The camp gives them two lanterns with four hours of oil in each, forty feet of rope and a crowbar, and Gerda says the four hours out loud as she hands them over. Serrin goes down with them and does not ask permission — he is at the shaft head when they turn round, holding one of the lanterns.

---

scenes.name: Five — The Standing Room
scenes.body:
The corridor runs on for forty feet past the chalk line and then opens out, and your lamplight goes into the opening and does not find the far wall.

The floor is the same fitted flagstone and it runs away from you into the dark in every direction you can see. The air is colder here again and it carries a mineral taste, like the back of a quarry.

And there are people standing on it.

Perhaps thirty of them. They are not gathered and they are not in a line — they are scattered across the whole width of the room at the easy irregular distances of people working near one another rather than standing together. Dwarves in mining leather with tools still in their hands. A woman in a long coat with one arm thrown up across her face. Two figures close together near the middle, one with a hand on the other's shoulder. Somebody small, off to the left, beside a pillar.

Every one of them is stone.

Nobody carved these. You know it immediately and you could not say exactly how — something about the way the cloth falls, which is the way cloth falls and not the way carved cloth falls, and something about the faces, which are not doing anything a sculptor would ever have chosen. One of the dwarves holds a pick whose wooden haft has rotted entirely away to a stub of punk in his grip, while the iron head and the stone fingers closed around it have stayed exactly where they were.

They are all facing the same way. Every single one of them. Away from the far end of the room.

Thirty people, caught mid-stride, every one of them turned to run.

> - [ ] Nothing moves for a full minute. No rolls until somebody asks a question, and the room holds while they do.

| When | Check | DC | What they get |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anyone walks up to one of them and looks at the face | Nature | any | These people were turned standing where they stood, and it is no curse you can put a name to |
| | | 12 | And not all on the same day. The dwarves are weathered — edges gone round, faces pitted, decades of still air working on them |
| | | 16 | The pair in the middle are not weathered at all — their cloth still has creases in it. That happened inside the last year, and they are wearing the same cut of leathers as the two men working the face up top |
| | | 20 | This can be undone. Not by anyone standing in this room and not quickly, but these are not corpses. They are people, and they are waiting |
| Anyone goes over to the small figure by the pillar | Investigation | any | Mining leathers, cut down and restitched to fit somebody a good deal smaller |
| | | 12 | They brought their children down here to work beside them, which tells you precisely how safe they believed this place to be |
| Anyone stops talking and listens to the dark ahead | Perception | any | The room swallows sound. No echo off a far wall, which means there is no far wall inside the range of anybody's voice |
| | | 11 | Not nothing. Something very large out there is breathing, slowly, and has been doing it the entire time you have been standing here |
| | | 15 | It is not asleep. The rhythm of it changed the moment your light came through that doorway |

> - [ ] Open floor among the figures. The paragraph below is for anyone who looks at what they are carrying, and however long they spend here, the light at the far end is the next thing anybody notices.

They are carrying everything they had on them when it happened. Belt pouches. Tool rolls. A woman with a ring of keys at her hip and a ledger under her arm. All of it stone, all of it fused to them, except where a strap has rotted through and let something drop — and there is a scatter of small objects lying loose on the flags around their feet, a hundred years of fastenings giving way, one at a time, in the dark.

> - [ ] On the flags, free to anyone who looks down: 35 gp in old dwarven coin, a short iron key with no lock left to fit, and a silver locket with a lock of hair in it still soft. Nothing comes off the figures themselves — it is part of them now. Anyone who made that Nature 20 knows these people are not dead, and pocketing the locket in front of a table that has just heard it is a scene in itself.

There is a light burning at the far end of the room, a long way off, and there are voices under it.

A dwarf woman is standing on a packing crate she has dragged up against the far wall, with a charcoal stick in her teeth and both hands flat on a sheet of hide pinned to the stone, working the charcoal across it in long even strokes. There are a dozen more hides finished and rolled at her feet, and she has been at this since yesterday morning.

Sitting against the wall beside the rolls, with his knees drawn up and a lamp beside him that burned out some hours ago, there is a young man in a carter's coat. He gets up so fast when your light reaches him that he nearly goes over.

**TAM:** "Oh thank every god. She will not come. I have asked her about forty times, I am not leaving her down here on her own, and I would very much like to leave. So. *Please.*"

**TAM:** "And before anybody asks — yes, it has been past us. Twice. It came to the edge of the light and it looked at us and it went away again, and I have not slept, and I would rather not be here when it changes its mind."

> - [ ] That is why they are alive. It is enormously old, it is not hungry, and two people standing still against a wall have not been interesting. Four more with lamps and steel are a different matter.

**DAZLYN:** (not turning round) "In a minute."

And behind them, set into the far wall, there is an arch.

Two uprights and a span, dwarf-cut and completely unornamented, standing a little over twice a man's height. And across the opening, filling it corner to corner, there is a slab of dressed stone — a gate, fitted into channels cut down both uprights, with a windlass and a counterweight chain rigged on the near side. The dwarves who built this room did not just build it around the arch. They built a door for it, and they shut it, and they left.

The arch is shut and it has been shut a very long time.

And something is still coming off it.

> - [ ] The memories arrive here, before the fight, with the gate still shut. Levi and Amryn separately, and neither of them knows what the arch is. No roll identifies it.

Levi — you are looking at a stone gate in a wall and you are suddenly somewhere else.

The hall at Aurelion. Your father's weight going out of him under your hands. Your brother's face across the body from you, lit from above, mouth open. And the ceiling *opening* — not breaking, opening — and the light coming down through it like something poured.

You have carried all of that for years. What you have never had, not once, is the next part. The gap between the light taking hold of you and waking in a field in a country you had never heard of has always been a blank you stopped picking at.

Standing here, in front of a shut door, the blank moves. Something is in it. You cannot see what yet.

Amryn — the same thing happens to you and it is nothing to do with him.

The laboratory. The pressure building in a containment ring you knew was underrated and used anyway. The elders' faces. Then the conclave floor, and your name being struck, and your family not being in the room for it, and the long walk out of the mountain with everything you owned on your back.

And then nothing. And then this coast.

You have told yourself for a hundred and fifteen years that you simply do not remember the journey, in the way that nobody remembers a hard road.

You are now extremely clear that there was no journey.

| When | Check | DC | What they get |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anyone climbs up beside her and looks at what she is copying | History | any | Dwarvish, cut close and regular, and there is a staggering amount of it — floor to ceiling, all four walls |
| | | 13 | Rotas, water allowances, a dispute over a spring that ran sixty years and outlived both the men having it. This is a parish register, not a scripture |
| | | 17 | The hand changes a third of the way along. A second mason took the work over and was not as good, and the spacing never recovers |
| Anyone examines the gate, the channels and the windlass | Investigation | any | A dressed slab riding in cut channels, counterweighted, rigged to be wound up and let down by one person |
| | | 12 | The channels are worn smooth and the chain is greased. This gate was opened and shut over and over for years before anybody decided to leave it down |
| | | 16 | The last thing done to it was done from this side and done to last — the windlass pawl has been hammered into its seat, and somebody then took the handle away with them. The handle is back on. It is new, and it is not dwarf-made |
| Anyone tries to get Dazlyn down off the crate and out | Persuasion | any | She says in a minute, and does not turn round, and keeps rubbing |
| | | 12 | She will leave if somebody else carries the rubbings. She will not leave the rubbings |
| | | 16 | Told plainly that the rubbings survive a cave-in and she does not, she stops, swears once, and starts packing |

> - [ ] Open floor at the far wall, and nothing comes out of the dark until they have had their look at the gate and at what she is copying. Tam will carry the finished rolls and has been waiting a day and a half for somebody to tell him he is allowed to. Neither Levi nor Amryn gets more than the feeling — the gate stays shut until Caelus opens it, halfway through the fight.

**DAZLYN:** (down the ladder, fast, when she sees where they are looking) "Don't touch the windlass.

I have had three months with that thing and I will tell you exactly what I know, which is nothing. Nothing has come out of it. Nothing has gone into it. They sealed it and they wrote four hundred feet of wall in this room and they do not mention it once, and the only thing I am sure of is that people who built like this did not shut a door for no reason."

And then, from somewhere out in the dark behind you, something very large stops breathing slowly and starts breathing quickly.

It comes forward into the edge of the lamplight one foot at a time.

It is the size of a cart horse and then some. Eight legs, splayed wide and set low, carrying a body built like a barrel of wet sand, and a hide of overlapping plates the colour of old liver that grate audibly against one another when it moves. It comes between the pillars rather than round them, and the plates along its back take the stone off both sides as it passes. It is enormously, patiently old, and it has had a very long time down here with nothing to do but grow and nothing at all to interrupt it.

It does not hurry. It has clearly never once had to.

> - [ ] Nobody in the party dies tonight. Petrification is the stake — grey creeping up a forearm, fingers going stiff and heavy, a hand that will not open. Slow, visible, and reversible.

> - [ ] Line of sight is the whole fight. Thirty standing bodies and a forest of pillars, and the answer is to fight from behind a petrified dwarf, there to be found rather than given. It goes for Emeric, Amryn and Kaelen first, being closer and lighter on their feet, which leaves Levi deciding whether to put himself in its line — standing still, in the open, looking at it.

> - [ ] Serrin does not fight. He moves between people keeping them upright and whole, in full view, while Tam gets Dazlyn behind a pillar and keeps her there, and she fights him about it the entire time.

---

scenes.name: Six — The Gate

images.name: the gate
images.file: Serrin Opens the Ancient Rune Gate.png

scenes.body:
> - [ ] This lands roughly halfway through the fight, on a round when the party are committed and nobody has a hand free.

Under the noise of it there is a sound nobody has time to place: a chain running out over a drum, slowly, and taking weight.

Serrin is at the far wall with both hands on the windlass.

He has been winding it for some time. The gate is already a third of the way up its channels and still rising, and the counterweight chain is going down past him link by link, and he is not hurrying about it either.

**SERRIN:** "Keep going. You are doing marvellously. Do not let me interrupt."

The slab clears the springing of the arch and keeps rising, and the gap underneath it fills with something that is not air.

The opening does not shimmer and it does not glow. It simply does not agree with the room around it. Lamplight falling through it arrives on the floor beyond in slightly the wrong place. The sound of the fight behind you comes back through it half a beat late and very slightly flattened. Looking at it directly for more than a few seconds makes the back of your eyes ache in a way that has nothing to do with the dark.

Levi — the blank fills in.

The light did not only take you. You were lifted out of your father's hall and so was the man kneeling opposite you, and you have spent years not remembering the one fact that was in front of your face the entire time.

Caelus came too.

And he lets go of the windlass, and turns round, and he is laughing — properly laughing, with his head back, the first entirely honest thing he has done in two days.

> - [ ] The disguise goes now, and it is not dramatic. The plain unremarkable face runs the way wax runs off a warm plate, and underneath it is Levi's own face — ten years harder, with a white scar through one eyebrow. The white goes out of the robe at the same time, from the collar downward, the way ink goes through water, until he is standing there in black from throat to boot. Everything about him is the same shape as the man in gold and none of it is the same colour.

> - [ ] How long Caelus has been in this world is open. Levi's sheet does not fix it and nothing here does either, so he speaks of it only as a long time and never puts a number on it. Set the gap wherever suits and he will not contradict it.

**CAELUS:** "All of it, and you did not know me on an empty road.

I was eight feet from you when it happened, Levi. Same hall, same floor, same light, same second — and I came down in a swamp four hundred miles south of where it put you, on my face, in the dark, with nothing. It took me years to find out there was a door at all, and everything after that to find where they put it. I have been in three courts and two prisons and I learned a trade I will not describe to you, and all of it to stand in this room.

You got a *field*. You got a road and a pleasant walk into a town where they gave you a sword and called you sir."

He puts the flat of his hand against the opening, and it holds his hand, the way water holds a hand.

**CAELUS:** "And this is the way back. Not a door *to* somewhere. A door *home* — it does not matter whose. Anyone who was not born in this country goes back to where they came from. I did not come to this room on a guess and I am not going to stand in a cave and argue it with a dwarf."

**DAZLYN:** (screaming it, from behind a pillar, over everything) "DON'T — don't you *dare* —

Nothing has gone in! Nothing has come out! Three months and not one thing in or out, and they sealed it and they built a room around it and they never wrote down *why* —

You do not know what it does when it opens! You do not know what it does to *this*!" (she hits the pillar beside her head with the flat of her hand) "You put something through that and this whole hill may come down on every one of us!"

**CAELUS:** (to Levi, pleasantly, not to her at all) "She may be right.

I came a very long way for it. You can have the rest of the mountain."

| When | Check | DC | What they get |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anyone sizes up the distance to him | — | free | Half the length of the room, a forest of pillars, thirty standing bodies and a basilisk somewhere in among them, and not one of you with a hand free |
| Somebody runs the floor anyway and grabs for him | Athletics | any | They get there. He is simply not where the hand closes, and he does not appear to move to arrange that |
| Somebody puts a spell or an arrow into him | — | any | It lands, and it hurts him. He looks down at the hole in the black robe, and then back up, and steps through regardless |
| Levi says anything at all to his brother | — | free | Caelus answers him, and answers properly, and does it kindly — which is a great deal worse than if he shouted |

> - [ ] Open floor, mid-fight, and the shortest pause of the night — everything they do here happens with a basilisk still in the room. There is no version where he is stopped, so what they choose is what they say to him, not whether he goes.

He steps backward through the arch.

The air closes over him the way the surface of a pond closes, and he is gone.

#### ↳ If Levi goes after him

You get a hand and most of a forearm through before it shuts.

It does not close the way the water closed over Caelus. It goes out like a lamp, all at once, and the edge of the opening comes down through your arm somewhere above the wrist with no more resistance than a thread parting — and then you are on your back on the flagstones with a stump at the end of your sleeve and no pain in it at all yet, and what is on the other side of that wall is your hand, and your brother, and the way home.

The pain arrives about three seconds later.

> - [ ] It takes the hand clean. No save, no roll — going after him is the choice and this is what the choice costs. He does not bleed out; the stump is cauterised to the bone. The healer who would have made short work of this went through the wall one second ahead of the hand, and that is not lost on anybody.

> - [ ] Levi stays in this realm. That is the whole point of the beat, and the hand is the price of having been one second behind his brother for the second time in his life.

#### ↳ If nobody goes after him

For about two seconds absolutely nothing happens.

Then the opening shuts.

---

Either way, it goes out like a lamp, and the pressure of it going out hits the room as a single hard shove — every loose thing on the floor jumps, the lamps all gutter at once, and a crack runs up the far wall from the arch to the ceiling with a noise like a tree coming apart.

And the ceiling of a hall that has not moved in a thousand years begins to come down.

---

scenes.name: Seven — Out

images.name: out
images.file: Collapsing Dwarven Gate in the Snowstorm.png

scenes.body:
The first thing to fall is the span of the arch itself, and the uprights go with it, and the far wall folds inward behind them.

The basilisk is directly underneath it.

It does not see it coming, because it is looking at you, and the whole weight of a dwarven ceiling takes it to the floor in one piece and there is nothing left of it to fight.

Then the rest of the roof starts.

> - [ ] Six rounds to the ladder, counted out. No initiative, no attacks of opportunity — just distance, choices and falling stone, roughly one complication a round: the corridor fills with dust until nobody can see past arm's length, a slab comes down across the chalk-line doorway and has to be gone over or round, one lamp goes out and the second is in somebody's teeth, and Dazlyn turns back for her rubbings — the dozen rolled hides at the foot of the crate, two days of copying, still lying where she was working.

> - [ ] The rubbings are the real one. She goes back for them, Tam goes after her, and somebody has to make that call in about four seconds. They come out if anyone goes for them, nobody in the party dies either way, and the price is being last up the ladder with the shaft dropping grit on your head.

The standing room goes first and you do not look back at it.

Thirty people who have been on their feet in that dark for longer than Phandalin has existed go down under their own ceiling, and the sound of it follows you up the corridor and catches you and goes past you, and then the corridor starts.

You come up that green-timber ladder in the dark with the rungs jumping under your hands, and the shaft pouring dust down onto your shoulders, and somebody above you shouting something you cannot hear a word of.

And then there are hands on your coat hauling you over the lip, and you are lying on frozen mud in grey afternoon light with the whole hillside groaning underneath you.

The shaft collapses about a minute later. It goes down with a long rolling thud you feel through the ground more than hear, and a column of dust stands up out of the hole and leans away east on the first wind of the day, and then there is nothing to look at.

---

scenes.name: Eight — Axeholm
scenes.body:
Nobody says anything for a while.

Don-Jon walks the length of the trench twice, looking at the ground, and comes back, and sits down on his crate at the lip of a shaft that is no longer a shaft, and takes out the pipe, and this time he lights it.

**DON-JON:** "Two seasons."

And after a long pull on it:

**DON-JON:** "Thirty-one years I have been putting holes in hillsides and I have never once seen one fill itself in behind me. I suppose that is the end of the claim, and I suppose Tradesmith will want a letter, and I find I do not much care about either."

He looks over at the lad.

**DON-JON:** "He came back up. That is the only part of today I will be telling anybody about."

> - [ ] Pay: Barthen's account, open-ended — no bill in that shop for as long as they work out of Phandalin. Don-Jon puts forty gold of his own on top because the lad came back up, and he will not discuss the forty gold.

> - [ ] Gerda gives them the good lantern and what is left of the oil, on the grounds that there is nothing left down there to light.

Tam is sitting on the step of Barthen's cart with a blanket round his shoulders, talking without pause to anybody who stands near him, and nobody has the heart to stop him.

And Dazlyn Grayshard is twenty feet away on her knees in the mud with the hides spread out in front of her, weighted at the corners with stones, going over them in the last of the light, and she has not spoken to anyone since the surface.

> - [ ] She got the rubbings out, or enough of them. If the hides were left behind, she read that last stretch yesterday and has it by heart, and the scene plays the same with her scratching it into the mud with a stick.

After a while she says, without looking up:

**DAZLYN:** "I have got the end of it.

The last stretch on that wall was cut in a hurry — shallow, bad spacing, and it stops in the middle of a sentence, and I could not make it fit with the rest of it because the rest of it is rotas and water rights and three generations of a man complaining about his brother-in-law.

It is an order. Somebody senior gave an order to close the hall and go, and whoever was cutting it did not get to finish writing it down."

She turns the hide round so you can see it, though none of you can read a word of it, and puts her finger on a single group of marks near the bottom.

**DAZLYN:** "That is a place name. It is the only one in four hundred feet of wall.

Axeholm.

It is a dwarven hold, it is two days north-west of here, and everyone has been perfectly sure for about two hundred years that there is nothing in it."

> - [ ] Axeholm is the next session. The hook is theirs to pick up or leave, and Dazlyn will be in Phandalin working on the hides either way.

The light goes off the top of the hills, and away north Icespire Peak holds its own grey lid of cloud exactly where it has held it every day you have been able to see it.

A day's ride west there is a town, and a shop in it, and a man behind the counter who is going to be extremely glad to see his cart.

Thirty feet under the hill behind you there is no room at all any more.

And somewhere a very great deal further away than either of those, a man with your face is walking home.

> - [ ] The session ends on that line. The ride back, and anyone asking Levi how he is, are the first scene of the next one.
